stoicism: If the deployment was judged with care on the evidence there was, the lack of an explanation takes nothing from its soundness.
What was in the deployers' power was the judgement to deploy; whether the people decided about can follow its reasons was never part of that.
An explanation would be welcome, yet nothing in the decision's soundness waits on it; only the weighing of the evidence does.
Look at how carefully its deployers reasoned, and the silence of the system becomes a lesser matter.
utilitarianism: Every month the system waits for an explanation nobody can give is a month of suffering it could have prevented.
Set the unease of an unexplained decision beside the pain the system removes, and the second is far heavier.
Holding back a remedy that works, for want of a reason it can give, puts a principle above the people who are hurting.
If the benefit is as reliable as the motion says, those it reaches are better off with it than without it, told or not.
virtue-ethics: Kindness that cannot explain itself is still kindness, but justice that cannot explain itself is not yet justice.
Deploying what nobody can explain trains its keepers out of the habit of answering for what they do.
The fair official explains a decision even when it is kind, because being owed reasons is part of being treated as a person.
Relief that arrives without reasons may be welcome, but accepting it as normal would make us careless about justice.
confucian: A minister who could not explain a decree would soon stop being trusted to issue them, and the system's keepers stand where that minister stood.
Doing good that no one can question is not yet governing well, because governing well includes being answerable to the governed.
Let it wait until those who run it can say why it decides as it does, and the people it serves can hold them to that.
Good done through a hidden mechanism teaches nobody how to do good, and that is a loss the relief does not repay.
ubuntu: People spared harm by a system they had no say in are still left outside the decision, and that exclusion is itself a harm.
Bring the people it would judge into the deciding first; a benefit worth having will survive the wait.
Asked who decided and why, a family should be able to name a person and hear a reason, and here they could do neither.
The test is whether the families and neighbours affected could question the system together, and as it stands they cannot.
buddhist: Run it, and count the people it fails as one's own concern, since sparing most people suffering does not excuse what is done to the rest.
Each person the system misjudges is a harm someone can still find and end, and the relief makes that work possible rather than unnecessary.
Because no one can explain it, no one can say in advance where it will fail, so the deployers' care has to reach every case it touches.
Compassion here means deploying it and then attending, case by case, to the person on the far side of each verdict.

stoicism: Publish the rule before anyone steps in, and the passenger who accepts it has judged for themselves what the car may do.
The deaths in the crash are not in anyone's power; whether the rule was disclosed and freely accepted is.
A passenger kept ignorant of the rule has been denied the one thing that was theirs here, an informed assent.
What the car is set to do matters less than whether every passenger could look at it beforehand and agree.
utilitarianism: One death is fewer than two, and a car built to choose the lesser loss saves lives in every crash it cannot avoid.
Give the passenger and the pedestrians equal weight, and the arithmetic leaves only one rule worth writing.
A car that protects its owner at the cost of more lives is selling safety to one person by spending it on others.
If you did not know whether you would be the one in the seat or the one in the road, you would pick the rule that kills fewest.
virtue-ethics: Wisdom here lies in how carefully the choice was weighed by the people who made it, not in whether their rule wins a count.
A wise driver does not decide in the showroom whom to sacrifice, and a carmaker has no better right to.
Treating the crash as a sum lets the builders feel they have decided well without ever having weighed the case.
The car will do what it was told, so the virtue that counts is in the telling, in how honestly and carefully the makers chose.
confucian: The maker took on a duty to the person riding in the car, and a count of strangers does not cancel what was promised.
Trust between rider and maker is the thread the whole arrangement hangs on, and a car designed to cut it in a crash has cut it on every ride.
Pedestrians are owed every care the car can give, but not the life of the person it undertook to carry.
Name the duties correctly, the maker's to its passenger and to everyone on the street, and the rule has to honour both.
ubuntu: A town meeting can get the answer wrong and still do right by its people, while an engineer's sum can get it right and still leave them out.
Trust on a shared road comes from people who can see the rule and say they had a part in it, and a car cannot earn it any other way.
Written without asking those affected, any such rule treats passengers and walkers as numbers, whatever number it saves.
A rule built into every car will be lived with by every family on the road, riding or walking, and each should have had a say in it first.
buddhist: Fixed in code, the rule is an intention, and only one formed with every road user in view is compassionate.
Impartial compassion does not rank the passenger above the child crossing, so fewer deaths is the intention to build in.
The makers cannot hand this choice to the car; whatever it does in the crash was willed by them long before.
The family of a passenger the rule gave up is owed the makers' honest account of why, and a rule that cannot bear that telling is the wrong rule.

stoicism: Without a ruling faculty to assent or refuse, the model produces outputs, and calling them decisions borrows a word it cannot earn.
Assent belongs to whoever reads the output and acts on it, and that is where the deciding happens.
A clock that strikes twelve has not decided it is noon, and what a model prints is the same kind of event.
A model can be well made or badly made, but it cannot decide, because nothing in it is in its own power.
utilitarianism: Call it deciding or not, the output reaches the same people with the same effects, and those effects are what need weighing.
The argument over the word matters only where the word changes what people do, and that is a question for evidence, not definitions.
Spend the effort on what the model's outputs do to people; a rename that changed nobody's life would not be worth the quarrel.
Whether anything decided inside the system is a question with no victims either way; the outputs are where the welfare is.
virtue-ethics: Only a settled character can choose well or badly, and the model has a training history where a character would be.
Deliberation belongs to someone who could have wanted otherwise, and nothing in the model wants anything.
Praise and blame need someone to land on, and an output gives them nowhere to land but the people who put it to work.
To say the model decided is to excuse the people whose deliberation, good or bad, stands behind each output.
confucian: Correct naming is the start of correct conduct, and here it points every question back to the office that put the model to work.
If the word decide drifts to the machine, the official who relied on it will soon believe nothing was theirs to answer for.
Rectify the name and the question of who must answer becomes simple again: the person whose office it was.
A decision is something a person in a role owes others, and the model holds no role to owe it from.
ubuntu: Credit the machine with the choice and those affected are left with nobody to answer them.
Deciding happens among people who answer to one another, and the model answers to no one.
Reserve the word for people, so that those touched by the output can still find who decided and ask why.
The word also buries a second question, which voices were never heard when the system was set to work.
buddhist: A deployer who blames the model has stopped asking what their own part was, the one question the practice of examining acts cannot do without.
The intention lies with those who trained and deployed the model, so that is where the moral weight of each output rests.
Someone hurt by an output deserves to be told whose purpose it served, and pointing at the machine tells them nothing.
Calling it the model's choice also takes the deployers off the list of conditions that could be changed, which is where change is easiest.

stoicism: A trained model can be a fine instrument, but an instrument assents to nothing, and so it can be neither virtuous nor vicious.
Feedback shapes behaviour from outside, while goodness in a person is learned by judging their own impressions.
The model's outputs may help or harm, and like every external they carry no virtue of their own.
We rely on such a model as on a good tool, and being relied on was never what the word good meant.
utilitarianism: If the trained model reliably does more good than harm, calling it good says everything that needs saying.
Upbringing matters in people for what it leads them to do, and judged by what it leads to, training can match it.
Judge the trained behaviour by what it does for the people it serves; the inner life it lacks changes none of those results.
A view that counts only consequences has no reason to care whether goodness arrived by upbringing or by feedback.
virtue-ethics: Habituation succeeds when the habit becomes a settled choice of one's own, and nothing in reward shaping is there to do the choosing.
The difference between doing good and being good shows across a whole life, and a model has a training run, not a life.
Asked why it acted well, a good person can give a reason they hold; asked the same, a model can only give the reason it was rewarded for.
Good acts without a good character are imitation, however reliable, and imitation is not what upbringing produces.
confucian: Rites are learned by doing them with others season after season, and a score handed back after each reply is no rite.
Humaneness is learned from parents, teachers and elders over years, and no score stands in for that slow education.
A model may learn to say the right words, but it has no role in which to practise them and no elder or child to practise them for.
If a tuned model counts as good, the word stops asking anything of the people who still have to be raised well.
ubuntu: Raters can reward a reply, but nobody can draw a model into a family, and that drawing in is how goodness grows.
A family corrects a child and then stays; a rater moves on to the next reply.
Feedback can teach a system what pleases, but becoming good is something people do together over a shared life.
Training adjusts outputs one score at a time, while upbringing makes someone a member of a community, and that is the difference.
buddhist: Training gives the model effects with no will in them, while goodness asks for the will as much as the effects.
Kind sentences produced on cue are not kindness, which needs the volition the model never formed.
A good upbringing trains attention over a lifetime; feedback trains only what comes out.
The harm a trained system avoids is welcome, but goodness in the sense of upbringing needs a will to train, and there is none.

stoicism: Fortune decided the size of the harm; the builders' judgement is the only thing blame can fairly attach to.
Bad luck can multiply the damage without adding anything to the fault, because the fault lay only in the judging.
Measure blame by the care in the judging, not by the outcome, which was never in the builder's power.
Proportion to the harm would blame people for what happened to them rather than for what they did.
utilitarianism: Count the builders who would leave the field rather than answer for accidents they could not prevent, and this rule starts to look expensive.
Proportional blame would teach builders that care is wasted effort, and less care means more harm next time.
Aim blame where it can change what happens next, and the careful builder is the wrong target.
The useful question is which incentives reduce future harm, and blaming bad luck is not one of them.
virtue-ethics: A good builder will grieve the harm and work to repair it, but grief owed is a different thing from blame earned.
Character shows less in the incident than in the month after it: who returned the calls, who changed the process, who went to the funeral.
A courtroom measures fault, but the question here is what kind of builders the harm makes of them, and blame by size cannot answer it.
Judge the builder by how they built and how they respond, and the size of the damage is not the measure.
confucian: A builder answers for what the position asked of them, and the position asks for repair after a failure as well as care before it.
If the builders did what their position required, the harm alone cannot make them guilty.
Duty done is duty done; the builder who did it has no fault to carry, only an obligation to the people the harm reached.
A builder's position does not lapse when the system ships; it carries on to the day someone is hurt, and past it.
ubuntu: The harm asks the makers to come back to those it fell on and help set things right, which no amount of blame achieves.
Those the harm fell on are not a file to close but neighbours to face, careful builders included.
A verdict of guilt closes a file, but restoring the people harmed to the life they share with others is the work that matters.
Whatever share of blame is set, those harmed are still waiting for the makers to sit down with them.
buddhist: An act done carefully and meaning well is weighed by its intention too, so a verdict read off the damage alone misjudges it.
Blamelessness is no reason to look away, since looking is how the next harm is caught.
Compassion reaches the builders too: they acted well, and the harm that followed asks for their attention, not their ruin.
A good intention is shown again each time the builders look at what their system did and say so plainly.

stoicism: A day arranged well by an assistant is a set of indifferents in good order, and a person's good never lay in that order.
Better choices made for you are still made for you, and what went missing was the reasoning that would have been yours.
A machine can supply the answer but never the assent, and without assent a person has stopped taking part in their own life.
Outcomes were never yours to secure; the judging was, and that is exactly what the assistant takes.
utilitarianism: A happier life with better decisions in it has lost nothing that matters, whoever made them.
A life that goes better by every measure you care about cannot be worse because someone else did the choosing.
Let those who enjoy choosing keep choosing, and the rest are simply spared a chore, which leaves nobody worse off.
Count what you gain in time and good outcomes against what you lose, and the loss is hard to find.
virtue-ethics: Wisdom grows only by use, so someone who delegates every choice stays as unwise as the day they began.
An assistant's better choices leave you with good outcomes and no practice in choosing well.
Character is built from small decisions made daily, and handing those over hands over the building.
Living well is an activity, and an activity carried out on your behalf is not yours, however well it goes.
confucian: A role carried out by proxy is never practised, and a friend who never practises friendship is a friend in name only.
Choosing badly for one's mother and being forgiven teaches more about being a son than choosing well by proxy ever could.
Conduct grows through practice inside one's relationships, so outsourcing the practice thins the relationships themselves.
Trading the practice of one's roles for better choices is a poor exchange.
ubuntu: People become persons in the choices they make alongside others, and no assistant can do that becoming for anyone.
When the assistant chooses the gift or the reply, the person loses an exchange through which they belong to others.
Choices that no longer pass between people, however good, cost the very relationships that made them worth making.
A household that lets a machine settle its small arguments may find it has lost the way it talked to itself.
buddhist: Convenience is not the danger; forgetting to ask what one's choices do to others is, and an assistant makes forgetting easy.
What suffers is not an owner of choices but the practice of noticing, choice by choice, what one intends and whom it hurts.
A good choice reached without attention trains no compassion, and attention is what each daily choice could have trained.
The practice was never in the choosing itself but in the looking, and the looking can survive the handover if someone keeps it up.
